summary: Every file has an owner and permissions that say who can read (r), write (w), and execute (x) it. chmod changes them. A script needs x before you can run it as ./script.
notes: -rw-r--r-- 1 student student reads as: a file; the owner (student) can read and write; the group and everyone else can only read.
In numbers, r = 4, w = 2, x = 1, added up for owner, group, others. 755 is rwxr-xr-x (a script) and 644 is rw-r--r-- (a normal file).
bash greet.sh works even without x because bash is the program being run, and it only needs to read the file.
pitfall: Running a script without the execute bit fails with Permission denied (in your own terminal: bash: ./greet.sh: Permission denied). Run chmod +x greet.sh once and try again.
setup_note: Starts with a two-line script named greet.sh that does not have execute permission.
